title: Finding an apartment
intro:
Most rentals go through a real-estate agency ({不動産屋[ふどうさんや]}). You browse listings online or in the shop, arrange a viewing ({内見[ないけん]}), apply, pass a screening ({審査[しんさ]}) and then sign the contract.

The upfront costs surprise many newcomers. Typical items include:

- {敷金[しききん]}: a deposit, used for cleaning and repairs when you move out; the rest is returned.
- {礼金[れいきん]}: key money, a non-refundable payment to the landlord. Many listings now have none.
- {仲介[ちゅうかい]手数料[てすうりょう]}: the agency's fee.
- The first month's rent, fire insurance, a lock change fee and a guarantor company fee.

Together these often add up to several months' rent, so budget carefully and ask for a full estimate.

Landlords usually want a guarantor ({保証人[ほしょうにん]}). Since most foreigners don't have a Japanese relative to ask, you will normally use a guarantor company ({保証[ほしょう]会社[がいしゃ]}) instead. Unfortunately, some landlords still refuse foreign tenants; agencies that specialize in helping foreigners can save you time.

Layouts are written as codes: the number is the count of rooms, plus K (kitchen), DK (dining-kitchen) or LDK (living-dining-kitchen). A 1R is a single room with the kitchen in it, 1K has a separate small kitchen, and 1LDK has a bedroom plus a living area. Room sizes are often given in tatami mats ({畳[じょう]}). Contracts commonly run for two years, and in some regions renewal requires a fee ({更新料[こうしんりょう]}).

phrases.jp: 部屋[へや]を探[さが]しているんですが。
家賃[やちん]は8万円[はちまんえん]以内[いない]がいいです。
phrases.en: I'd like the rent to be 80,000 yen or less.

phrases.jp: 駅[えき]から徒歩[とほ]10分[じゅっぷん]以内[いない]がいいです。
phrases.en: I'd prefer within a 10-minute walk of the station.

phrases.jp: 外国人[がいこくじん]でも借[か]りられますか。
礼金[れいきん]なしの物件[ぶっけん]はありますか。
phrases.en: Are there any places with no key money?

phrases.jp: 初期[しょき]費用[ひよう]は全部[ぜんぶ]でいくらぐらいですか。
phrases.en: About how much are the move-in costs in total?

phrases.jp: 管理費[かんりひ]は含[ふく]まれていますか。
内見[ないけん]できますか。
保証人[ほしょうにん]がいないんですが。
保証[ほしょう]会社[がいしゃ]を利用[りよう]できますか。
phrases.en: Can I use a guarantor company?

phrases.jp: バス・トイレ別[べつ]ですか。
phrases.en: Are the bath and toilet separate?

phrases.jp: 契約[けいやく]期間[きかん]は何年[なんねん]ですか。
更新料[こうしんりょう]はかかりますか。
退去[たいきょ]するときは、いつまでに連絡[れんらく]すればいいですか。
phrases.en: How much notice do I need to give when moving out?

vocab.jp: 不動産屋[ふどうさんや]
仲介[ちゅうかい]手数料[てすうりょう]
保証[ほしょう]会社[がいしゃ]
更新料[こうしんりょう]

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.jp: いらっしゃいませ。お部屋[へや]をお探[さが]しですか。
dialogue.en: Welcome. Are you looking for an apartment?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: はい。会社[かいしゃ]の近[ちか]くで、1Kか1DKの部屋[へや]を探[さが]しています。
dialogue.en: Yes. I'm looking for a 1K or 1DK near my office.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.jp: ご予算[よさん]はどのくらいでしょうか。

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 管理費[かんりひ]込[こ]みで7万円[ななまんえん]ぐらいです。
dialogue.en: Around 70,000 yen including the maintenance fee.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.jp: かしこまりました。こちらの物件[ぶっけん]はいかがでしょうか。駅[えき]から徒歩[とほ]8分[はっぷん]で、築[ちく]10年[じゅうねん]です。
dialogue.en: Certainly. How about this one? It's an 8-minute walk from the station and the building is 10 years old.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: いいですね。外国人[がいこくじん]でも大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]ですか。
dialogue.en: Looks good. Is it OK for a foreigner?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.jp: はい。保証[ほしょう]会社[がいしゃ]のご利用[りよう]が条件[じょうけん]ですが、問題[もんだい]ございません。
dialogue.en: Yes. Using a guarantor company is a condition, but that's no problem.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 初期[しょき]費用[ひよう]はどのくらいかかりますか。
dialogue.en: How much will the move-in costs be?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.jp: 敷金[しききん]1ヶ月[いっかげつ]、礼金[れいきん]なしなので、全部[ぜんぶ]で家賃[やちん]の4ヶ月分[よんかげつぶん]ぐらいです。
dialogue.en: Deposit is one month and there's no key money, so in total about four months' rent.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 内見[ないけん]できますか。

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.jp: はい、今日[きょう]の午後[ごご]でしたらご案内[あんない]できます。
dialogue.en: Yes, I can take you this afternoon.

tips: Take photos of every scratch and stain on move-in day and send them to the agency. It helps when the deposit is settled at move-out.
One tatami mat is roughly 1.5 to 1.7 square meters depending on the region. A 6-mat room is small by many Western standards.
Read the move-out notice period in your contract; one month is common, but check.
Ask whether the place comes with lights, air conditioning and a gas stove. Unfurnished in Japan can mean very bare.
Share houses and furnished monthly apartments are an easy first step while you get your bank account, phone and job sorted out.
